a: Your calf, Samaria, he has thrown away.
t: He threw it away, or throw it away?
p: The Hebrew has 'he has rejected your calf'. The Greek has a command: 'Throw away your calf, Samaria.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); Aleppo Codex
readings.en: he has rejected your calf, Samaria
readings.plain: Your calf, Samaria, he has thrown away.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: throw away your calf, Samaria
readings.plain: Throw away your calf, Samaria.

why: The Hebrew verb is a normal perfect, 'he has rejected', and the Masoretic pointing agrees with the sense of the next lines (my anger burns against them). The Greek reads the same consonants as an imperative, which would make Samaria the one who must throw away the calf. A few modern commentators prefer it because 'he' has no clear subject. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: Though I write for him the many points of my law
t: Many points, or ten thousand?
p: The verb is the same in the line and in the margin note (both 'I write'), only spelled two ways. The real difference is the next word: the consonants say 'ten thousand', the margin says 'many things'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (the Qere, the reading the margin tells the reader to say)
readings.en: I write for him the many things of my law
readings.plain: Though I write for him the many points of my law

readings.w: Masoretic Text, the Ketiv (the consonants as written in the line)
readings.en: I write for him ten thousand [things] of my law
readings.plain: Though I write for him ten thousand points of my law

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: I will write down for him a multitude
readings.plain: I will write out for him a multitude of my laws

why: The Ketiv and the Qere have the same verb, an imperfect ('I write' or 'I would write'), spelled 'ektov in the line and 'ektav in the margin; that is spelling only. They differ in the next word: 'ten thousand' (ribbo) or 'many things' (rubbe). The Qere's 'many things' is a plain statement; the Ketiv and the Greek lean toward a large number. The Greek verb is a future ('I will write down'), which fits the imperfect. A simple past ('I wrote') is not what the Hebrew says, so the Plain reads the imperfect as 'though I write'. The Plain follows the margin for the noun.

a: Ephraim was like Tyre
t: Like Tyre, or for hunting?
p: The Hebrew says 'to Tyre' or 'like Tyre'. The Greek has 'for prey' or 'for the hunt'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), words partly restored
readings.orig: אֶפְרַיִם כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאִיתִי לְצוֹר שְׁתוּלָה בְנָוֶה
readings.en: Ephraim, as I have seen, [is] planted to Tyre in a meadow
readings.plain: Ephraim was like Tyre

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: Ἐφράιμ ὃν τρόπον εἰς θήραν παρέστησαν τὰ τέκνα αὐτῶν
readings.en: Ephraim, as they set their children for the hunt
readings.plain: As Ephraim set out his children for the hunt

why: The Hebrew words look alike (tsor, Tyre, and tsayid, hunting) and the Greek translator may have read a different word, or a different text may lie behind it. The Hebrew line is hard (what does 'as I have seen' do?), and this is why a few commentators prefer the Greek: 'Ephraim, as I have seen, brings his children out for the hunter'. The Masoretic Text makes sense as a comparison with a well-placed city, and the Plain keeps it. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg has the verse, but the word in question is restored in the transcription, so it cannot be cited.

a: Israel is a luxuriant vine
t: Luxuriant, empty or plundering?
p: The Hebrew word boqeq can mean 'luxuriant', 'empty' or 'plundering'. The Greek takes the first sense.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves these words
readings.en: Israel is a boqeq vine
readings.plain: Israel is a luxuriant vine

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: Israel is a vine rich in branches
readings.plain: Israel is a vine full of branches

why: Both witnesses have the same Hebrew word; the Greek translator chose a sense for it (euklematousa, 'with good vine shoots'), so this is a difference in meaning, not in text. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves gefen boqeq Yisra'el with nothing restored, so the consonants were the same by the Dead Sea period. The three senses are laid out in the note. The Plain keeps 'luxuriant' because the next clause says the vine bore fruit.

a: the heifers of Beth-aven
t: Heifers of Beth-aven or the calf of Beth-On?
p: The Hebrew has 'heifers', plural, and 'Beth-aven'. The Greek has one calf and 'Beth-On'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), partly restored
readings.en: the heifers of Beth-aven
readings.plain: the heifers of Beth-aven

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: the calf of the house of On
readings.plain: the calf of Beth-On

why: The Hebrew plural 'heifers' may be a plural of majesty for a single image (compare Exodus 32:4, 8, where one calf is called 'gods'). The Greek reads the singular and writes 'On' (the Egyptian city) for 'aven'; the two Hebrew words differ only in one letter. 'Beth-aven' is Hosea's own play on Bethel (4:15; 5:8), and the Plain keeps it. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves the beginning of the line and agrees with the Masoretic Text, though 'house of wickedness' itself is restored.

a: King Jareb
t: King Jareb, or King Iareim?
p: The Hebrew says 'King Jareb'. The Greek writes 'King Iareim'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves these words
readings.en: to King Jareb
readings.plain: King Jareb

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: to King Iareim
readings.plain: King Jareim

why: The scroll 4QXIIg preserves lemelekh yarev with nothing restored, so the Hebrew name stood in the text by the Dead Sea period. The Greek ends the name in -m here and at 5:13, which may be a different reading or only the translator's guess at an unknown name. The name is not known from Assyrian records; the note lists the guesses. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: their two guilts
t: Two guilts or two eyes?
p: The Hebrew line has 'two eyes' in the consonants and 'two iniquities' in the margin. The Greek has 'iniquities'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex, the Qere (the margin)
readings.en: their two iniquities
readings.plain: their two guilts

readings.w: Masoretic Text, the Ketiv (the consonants of the line)
readings.en: their two eyes
readings.plain: their two eyes

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: in their two iniquities
readings.plain: their two guilts

why: The Ketiv 'two eyes' makes no obvious sense in the picture (bound to their two eyes?), while 'two iniquities' fits the context of sin and discipline, and the Greek agrees with the Qere. Some read the consonants as 'eyes' in the sense of 'springs' and others as 'furrows'. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves only the first words of the verse ('and they will be gathered against them'). 'Peoples', 'bound', 'two' and 'iniquities' are all restored in the transcription, so the scroll cannot be cited for the disputed phrase.

a: Judah will plow
t: Judah will plow, or 'I will be silent about Judah'?
p: The Hebrew says Judah will plow. The Greek says 'I will keep silent about Judah'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves these words without restoration
readings.en: Judah will plow; Jacob will break up the ground for himself
readings.plain: Judah will plow

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: I will keep silent about Judah; Jacob will be strong for him
readings.plain: I will say nothing about Judah

why: The Greek seems to have read yacharosh ('he will plow') as yacharish ('he will be silent'); the two differ by one vowel letter. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves yacharosh Yehudah yesadded lo Ya'aqov with nothing restored and agrees with the Masoretic Text, and the three workers Ephraim, Judah and Jacob match each other in the Hebrew. The scroll also preserves 'loved to thresh' earlier in the verse, where the Greek has 'loved strife'. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: as Shalman plundered Beth-arbel
t: Beth-arbel, or the house of Jeroboam?
p: The Hebrew has 'Shalman' and 'Beth-arbel'. The Greek has 'Salaman, a ruler from the house of Jeroboam'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: like the plundering of Shalman, Beth-arbel
readings.plain: as Shalman plundered Beth-arbel

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ὡς ἄρχων Σαλαμὰν ἐκ τοῦ οἴκου Ἰεροβοάμ
readings.en: like the ruler Salaman from the house of Jeroboam
readings.plain: as a ruler named Shalman from the house of Jeroboam did

why: The Greek seems to have read 'Beth-arbel' (beit arbel) as 'Beth-Jeroboam' (beit yarov'am) or to have understood 'Arbel' as a ruler's name. The Masoretic Text reads as a normal comparison with a famous attack on a named place. The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg has 'Beth-arbel' but the name is restored in the transcription, so the scroll cannot be cited for it.

a: and I called my son out of Egypt
t: My son, or his children?
p: The Hebrew has 'my son'. The Greek has 'his children'. Matthew 2:15 follows the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), where the word 'my son' is restored
readings.en: and from Egypt I called my son
readings.plain: and I called my son out of Egypt

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus); some Hebrew scholars think the translator read a plural
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου μετεκάλεσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and out of Egypt I called his children
readings.plain: and I called his children out of Egypt

why: The Hebrew libni ('my son') is the reading Matthew quotes, and the Plain follows it. The Greek 'his children' may come from a different Hebrew text or from a loose rendering; it is not clear. The Greek line also begins with a few words that belong to the end of the Hebrew 10:15.
b: The transcription of 4QXIIg shows 'my son' only as a restored word, so the scroll is not cited as a witness for it.

a: They called to them; they walked away from them.
t: They called, or I called?
p: The Hebrew says 'They called to them', with no named caller. The Greek has 'As I called them, so they went away from me'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves 'to them, so they went from before them' without restoration
readings.en: they called to them; so they went from before them
readings.plain: They called to them; they walked away from them.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καθὼς μετεκάλεσα αὐτούς, οὕτως ἀπῴχοντο ἐκ προσώπου μου
readings.en: as I called them, so they went away from my face
readings.plain: As I called them, so they walked away from me.

why: The Hebrew leaves the callers unnamed: prophets, priests or the LORD's messengers. The Greek makes the LORD the caller, which follows from 11:1 ('I called my son'). The Greek reading needs a first-person verb and a different ending in Hebrew ('I called' and 'from me'), and the Masoretic Text is the harder reading. It is also the more natural in the Hebrew style of the chapter, where the LORD first speaks of the past in the third person. The Plain follows it. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves lahem ken halkhu mippenehem unrestored, so the Hebrew 'from before them' is old, and the Greek 'from my face' is a different text or a free rendering.

a: taught Ephraim to walk
t: Taught to walk, or bound the feet?
p: The Hebrew verb is rare and means 'I made walk'. The Greek has 'I shackled Ephraim's feet'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), the verb restored
readings.en: and I, I taught Ephraim to walk
readings.plain: taught Ephraim to walk

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and I bound together Ephraim's feet
readings.plain: tied Ephraim's feet

why: The Hebrew tirgalti is a rare verb from regel, 'foot', and the sense 'taught to walk' fits the arms of the next line. The Greek verb means 'to hobble, fetter', which fits neither the arms nor the healing that follows. The Greek translator probably did not know the Hebrew word and guessed from the root. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: To the land of Egypt they will not return
t: Not Egypt, or Egypt?
p: The Hebrew says they will not return to Egypt. The Greek says Ephraim lived in Egypt.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), partly restored
readings.en: he will not return to the land of Egypt
readings.plain: To the land of Egypt they will not return

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: Ephraim lived in Egypt
readings.plain: Ephraim lived in the land of Egypt

why: The Greek has no negative and reads a different verb ('lived'). It agrees with the lines in 8:13 and 9:3 where the people do go back to Egypt. The Hebrew can be read as a flat denial ('but Assyria will be their king'), as a question ('Will they not return to Egypt?'), or as the stress that Egypt is not the place of exile and Assyria is. The Masoretic Text's wording is the harder and stays in the Plain.

a: hang on to their turning away from me
t: Turning away, or dwelling?
p: The Hebrew word meshuvah means 'turning away'. The Greek seems to read 'dwelling'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves 'and my people hang on to my turning away, and to One Above they call' without restoration
readings.en: and my people are hung to their turning away from me
readings.plain: hang on to their turning away from me

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ ὁ λαὸς αὐτοῦ ἐπικρεμάμενος ἐκ τῆς κατοικίας αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and his people hang from his dwelling
readings.plain: hang from their dwelling

why: The Greek has 'dwelling' (katoikia), the same word it uses for 'turning away' at 14:4; the translator seems to have taken meshuvah from the root 'sit, dwell' in both places. The rest of the Greek verse is also loose. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves le-meshuvati with nothing restored, so the Masoretic Text's word is old. The Plain follows it and keeps 'turning away' to match 14:4 and Jeremiah 3:22.

a: But Judah still roams with God, with the Holy One who is faithful.
t: Judah roams, or God knows them?
p: The Hebrew speaks of Judah and the Holy One. The Greek says 'Now God has known them, and a holy people will be called God's'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves 'with lying Ephraim, and with deceit the house' and 'and with holy ones, faithful' without restoration
readings.orig: וִיהוּדָה עֹד רָד עִם־אֵל וְעִם־קְדוֹשִׁים נֶאֱמָן
readings.en: and Judah still roams with God and with holy ones, faithful
readings.plain: But Judah still roams with God, with the Holy One who is faithful.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: νῦν ἔγνω αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός, καὶ λαὸς ἅγιος κεκλήσεται θεοῦ
readings.en: now God has known them, and a holy people will be called God's
readings.plain: Now God knows them, and a holy people will be called God's.

why: The Greek has no Judah in this verse, takes 'rad' as 'knew' and 'holy ones' as 'a holy people'. It makes the verse a sentence of hope, an anticipation of 11:10-11. The Masoretic Text speaks of Judah, as the 'case against Judah' of 12:2 requires, and the Plain follows it. The Greek line may come from a different Hebrew text, or from a loose and hopeful reading of the hard Hebrew. The scroll agrees with the Masoretic Text in the plural 'holy ones' (qedoshim) and in rad, against the Greek 'a holy people'; its words for Israel, Judah and 'God' are restored.

a: and there he spoke with us.
t: He found him and spoke with us, or they found me?
p: The Hebrew line says 'there he spoke with us'. The Greek line has 'they found me ... and there it was spoken to them'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), partly restored
readings.en: and there he spoke with us
readings.plain: and there he spoke with us.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus); the verb 'found' goes with the line before
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ Ὤν εὕροσάν με, καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτούς
readings.en: in the house of On they found me, and there it was spoken to them
readings.plain: and there it was spoken to them.

why: The Greek translated 'he found him' of the line before as 'they found me' and 'with us' as 'to them'. This turns the story back to the third person: what God said at Bethel was said to Jacob and his sons, not to 'us'. The Hebrew keeps the shift from the ancestor to the audience ('with us'), which is the point of the line. Some commentators suggest a different Hebrew text behind the Greek, others a loose rendering. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: If Gilead is wicked
t: Gilead and Gilgal, or Gilead twice?
p: The Greek has Gilead twice, 'rulers' for 'bulls' and 'turtles' for 'heaps'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves 'in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls' and 'on the furrows of a field' without restoration
readings.orig: אִם־גִּלְעָד אָוֶן אַךְ־שָׁוְא הָיוּ בַּגִּלְגָּל שְׁוָרִים זִבֵּחוּ גַּם מִזְבְּחוֹתָם כְּגַלִּים עַל תַּלְמֵי שָׂדָי
readings.en: If Gilead is wickedness, surely they are worthless; in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars too are like heaps on the furrows of a field
readings.plain: If Gilead is wicked

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: εἰ μὴ Γαλαάδ ἐστιν, ἄρα ψευδεῖς ἦσαν ἐν Γαλαὰδ ἄρχοντες θυσιάζοντες, καὶ τὰ θυσιαστήρια αὐτῶν ὡς χελῶναι ἐπὶ χέρσον ἀγροῦ
readings.en: If Gilead is not there, then they were false; in Gilead rulers sacrificing, and their altars like turtles on a barren field
readings.plain: If Gilead is not there

why: The Greek has no Gilgal, reads shorim ('bulls') as sarim ('rulers'; the two differ by a vowel letter), and has chelonai ('turtles') where the Hebrew has gallim ('heaps'); where that last word comes from is unclear. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves 'in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls' and 'on the furrows of a field' without restoration, so Gilgal and 'bulls' are old, and the sound-play on Gilgal and gallim (see the note) belongs to the Hebrew. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves.
t: Kiss calves, or 'the calves have run out'?
p: The Hebrew says sacrificers 'kiss calves'. The Greek says 'Sacrifice people, for the calves have run out'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: sacrificers of humans, calves they kiss
readings.plain: Those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: sacrifice humans, for the calves have failed
readings.plain: Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have run out.

why: The Greek made 'those who sacrifice' an imperative (thysate, 'sacrifice!') and has 'for the calves have run out' (ekleloipasin, 'have failed'). It is not clear what Hebrew lies behind 'run out': the Hebrew verb nashaq means 'kiss' (a second root, 'be armed', is in Psalm 78:9), so the Greek may reflect a different text or a free rendering. Its result is a bitter joke: people are offered when bulls are lacking. The Hebrew 'kiss' is a well-known act of homage (1 Kings 19:18). The Plain follows the Masoretic Text as a plain statement and adds no command; the note sets out the other readings of the line.

a: But I have been the LORD your God since the land of Egypt.
t: The shorter Hebrew, or the longer text?
p: The Masoretic Text is short. The Greek and a Dead Sea scroll add a line about creating the heavens and the host of heaven.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: and I [have been] the LORD your God from the land of Egypt
readings.plain: But I have been the LORD your God since the land of Egypt.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ δὲ Κύριος ὁ θεός σου, στερεῶν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ κτίζων γῆν, οὗ αἱ χεῖρες ἔκτισαν πᾶσαν τὴν στρατείαν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ οὐ παρέδειξά σοι αὐτὰ τοῦ πορεύεσθαι ὀπίσω αὐτῶν· καὶ ἐγὼ ἀνήγαγόν σε ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου
readings.en: But I am the LORD your God, who makes the heavens firm and creates the earth, whose hands made the whole army of the sky, and I did not show them to you, for you to walk after them. And I brought you up out of the land of Egypt
readings.plain: But I have been the LORD your God, who made the heavens firm and created the earth, whose hands made the whole army of the sky. I did not show them to you, for you to walk after them. And I brought you up out of the land of Egypt.

readings.w: 4QXIIc (4Q78), the words it preserves (some of the words between are restored)
readings.orig: אנוכי יהוה … בצר שמים … ארץ אשר ידיו ברא כול צבא השמים ולוא הראיתים לכה ללכת אחריהמה … העלותיכה … מצרים
readings.en: I [am] the LORD … [bṣr] the heavens … the earth, whose hands created all the host of the heavens, and I did not show them to you, to walk after them … I brought you up … Egypt
readings.plain: I am the LORD … the heavens … the earth, whose hands made the whole army of the sky. I did not show them to you, for you to walk after them. … I brought you up out of the land of Egypt.

why: The longer text is attested in the Greek and in 4QXIIc, which has the same plus with small differences in wording. Some scholars take it as the original and the shorter Masoretic Text as a loss; others take it as an expansion drawing on Isaiah 45:12 and Deuteronomy 4:19, with the teaching that the sun, moon and stars are made by the LORD and not to be followed. The short text matches 12:9 word for word, which some take as a sign that it is the original here. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and shows the longer reading as a variant.
b: The plus puts an explicit statement about creation in the middle of the verse: the host of heaven (sun, moon and stars) are made by the LORD and are not to be followed. The same worry is in Deuteronomy 4:19 and in 2 Kings 17:16. In the scroll the first word of the plus is written bṣr; the Greek has 'who makes firm' (stereon), which suggests a verb of that sense, but the Hebrew form is not clear. The scroll's word for 'and creates' is restored.

a: I knew you
t: I knew you, or I shepherded you?
p: The Hebrew says 'I knew you'. The Greek says 'I shepherded you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIc (4Q78), which preserves 'I knew you in the wilderness' (spelled yeda'tikha, a spelling difference only)
readings.en: I knew you in the wilderness
readings.plain: I knew you

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ ἐποίμαινόν σε ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
readings.en: I shepherded you in the wilderness
readings.plain: I shepherded you

why: The Greek verb means 'tend as a shepherd'. It may translate a different Hebrew verb (ra'ah, 'shepherd') or may be a free way of rendering 'know' as 'care for'. The scroll 4QXIIc preserves 'I knew you' (spelling aside), so the verb of the Masoretic Text is old. The Plain follows it; 'know' is already a word of care in Hosea (see the note).

a: Like a leopard I will watch beside the road.
t: I will watch, or the road of Assyria?
p: The Hebrew letters can be read 'I will watch' or 'Assyria'. The Greek reads Assyria.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: like a leopard on the road I will watch
readings.plain: Like a leopard I will watch beside the road.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ὡς πάρδαλις κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν Ἀσσυρίων
readings.en: like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians
readings.plain: Like a leopard I will lie in wait on the road to Assyria.

why: The same four letters mean 'I will watch' (with the vowels of the Masoretic Text) and 'Assyria'. The Greek reads 'the way of the Assyrians', which fits the exile route and the political setting of the chapter. The Hebrew vowels make a verb that matches the leopard's behavior, and it echoes the LORD's 'watching over' in 14:8, which is why the Plain keeps it. The words are restored in both Dead Sea transcriptions that cover the verse, so the scrolls give no help.

a: like a lioness
t: A lioness, or lions of the forest?
p: The Hebrew says 'like a lioness'. A Dead Sea scroll and the Greek have 'of the forest'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.orig: וָאֹכְלֵם שָׁם כְּלָבִיא חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה תְּבַקְּעֵם
readings.en: and I will devour them there like a lioness; a wild animal of the field will split them
readings.plain: like a lioness

readings.w: 4QXIIc (4Q78), in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (the two words marked as differing from the Masoretic Text)
readings.orig: ואכלום שם כלבי היער חית [השדה] תבקעם
readings.en: and I will devour them there like lions of the forest; a wild animal of [the field] will split them
readings.plain: like lions of the forest

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καταφάγονται αὐτοὺς ἐκεῖ σκύμνοι δρυμοῦ, θηρία ἀγροῦ διασπάσει αὐτούς
readings.en: young lions of the forest will devour them there; wild animals of the field will tear them
readings.plain: young lions of the forest

why: The scroll and the Greek both have 'of the forest', which the Masoretic Text does not, so a different Hebrew line probably lies behind both. Which is earlier cannot be told from three witnesses: 'lioness' (lavi') is the rarer word and fits the list of beasts in 13:7-8, while 'lions of the forest' could be a fuller, easier reading. The word division of the scroll's first word is the editors' of the transcription. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves only the first words of the verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: Where is that king of yours?
t: 'Where' spelled two ways
p: The Masoretic Text spells the word for 'where' so that it looks like 'I will be'. A Dead Sea scroll spells it the usual way.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: where [is] your king then
readings.plain: Where is that king of yours?

readings.w: 4QXIIc (4Q78), which preserves the word without restoration
readings.en: where [is] your king then
readings.plain: Where is that king of yours?

why: The Masoretic Text writes 'ehi for 'where' here and at 13:14; the usual spelling is 'ayyeh, which is what 4QXIIc has at 13:10. The Greek (pou) and the Latin (ubi) also read 'where' here, so there is no difference of sense at 13:10. At 13:14 the same Masoretic spelling could also be read 'I will be', as the Latin does; the scroll does not preserve 13:14 (see the note there). The 4QXIIc form at 13:10 is the best Hebrew support for reading the Masoretic form as 'where'.

a: Should I ransom them from the hand of Sheol?
t: A question, or 'I will ransom them'?
p: The Hebrew has no mark of a question. The Greek reads this line and the next as statements: 'I will ransom ... I will redeem'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: from the hand of Sheol will I ransom them?
readings.plain: Should I ransom them from the hand of Sheol?

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus); the Latin of Jerome's Vulgate also takes it as a promise
readings.en: from the hand of Hades I will deliver them
readings.plain: I will ransom them from the hand of Sheol.

why: The question form is a reading of the unpointed Hebrew, which has no interrogative letter; the Greek and the Latin make it a promise. The following lines are the same: see the entry on the next line. The Plain keeps the questions because the Hebrew allows both and the context (13:12-16) leans toward threat, but the note and the card lay out the other readings. The verb for ransom here (padah) is the one of Exodus 13:13 and Psalm 49:15. The two 'Where' questions of the next lines turn on the word 'ehi, which can also be read 'I will be': see the note on that word.

a: Should I redeem them from death?
t: A question, or 'I will redeem them'?
p: This line goes with the one before it. The Greek reads it as a promise.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008)
readings.en: from death will I redeem them?
readings.plain: Should I redeem them from death?

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus); the Latin of Jerome's Vulgate also takes it as a promise
readings.en: and from death I will redeem them
readings.plain: I will redeem them from death.

why: See the entry on the line before. The two lines are read together: both questions, or both promises. The Dead Sea scrolls do not preserve the verse.

a: let us pay you the bulls of our lips.
t: Bulls of our lips, or fruit of our lips?
p: The Hebrew says 'bulls'. The Greek says 'fruit'. Hebrews 13:15 follows the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); Jerome's Latin ('the calves of our lips')
readings.en: and let us pay bulls, our lips
readings.plain: let us pay you the bulls of our lips.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus); Hebrews 13:15 follows it
readings.en: and we will repay the fruit of our lips
readings.plain: and we will repay you with the fruit of our lips.

why: The Hebrew parim ('bulls') and the Greek 'fruit' (peri in Hebrew letters) differ by a single letter. A common explanation is that a mem was added or dropped in copying. The bulls reading is the harder and has the oddness of lips as bulls; it is the one Jewish tradition kept ('the bulls of our lips', words as sacrifice). The Greek 'fruit' is smoother and became the reading of Hebrews 13:15. The scroll 4QXIIc (4Q78) has the verse with the word for 'bulls' restored in the transcription, so it does not settle the question. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: I will heal their turning away.
t: Turning away, or dwelling?
p: The Hebrew says 'their turning away'. The Greek says 'I will heal their dwellings'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIc (4Q78), which preserves 'their turning away' without restoration
readings.en: I will heal their turning away
readings.plain: I will heal their turning away.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus) (its verse 14:5)
readings.en: I will heal their dwellings
readings.plain: I will heal their homes.

why: The Greek seems to have read the same letters in a different order, moshavotam ('their dwellings') for meshuvatam; it uses the same word at 11:7. The scroll 4QXIIc preserves meshuvatam with nothing restored, so the Masoretic Text's word is old. The Hebrew also fits Jeremiah 3:22, 'I will heal your turning away'. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: I have answered him, and I will watch over him.
t: I answered, or I humbled him?
p: The Hebrew verb is 'I answered'. The Greek has 'I humbled him and will strengthen him'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82), which preserves 'I have answered and I will watch him' without restoration
readings.en: I have answered and I will watch him
readings.plain: I have answered him, and I will watch over him.

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ ἐταπείνωσα αὐτόν, καὶ κατισχύσω αὐτόν
readings.en: I humbled him, and I will strengthen him
readings.plain: I humbled him, and I will make him strong.

why: The Hebrew 'aniti can come from 'anah I, 'answer', or 'anah II, 'afflict, humble'; the Greek took the second. For 'I will watch over him' ('ashurennu) the Greek has 'I will strengthen him', perhaps reading another verb. The Hebrew 'answer' fits the picture of the LORD responding to Ephraim's prayer in 14:2-3. And the verb 'I will watch' returns the word of 13:7, where the leopard 'watches' the road. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The scroll 4QXIIg preserves exactly the disputed words ('aniti va'ashurennu) and agrees with the Masoretic Text, so the Greek 'humbled' and 'strengthen' do not come from a Hebrew text found at Qumran.
